Hugging Face on AMD Instinct MI300 GPU

📅 21 May 2024 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Join the next Hugging Cast on June 6th to ask questions to the post authors, watch a live demo deploying Llama 3 on MI300X on Azure, plus a bonus demo deploying models locally on Ryzen AI PC!
  • Register at https://streamyard.com/watch/iMZUvJnmz8BV.
  • Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we want to make it easy to build AI with open models and open source, whichever framework, cloud and stack you want to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join the next Hugging Cast on June 6th to ask questions to the post authors, watch a live demo deploying Llama 3 on MI300X on Azure, plus a bonus demo deploying models locally on Ryzen AI PC!

Register at https://streamyard.com/watch/iMZUvJnmz8BV.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we want to make it easy to build AI with open models and open source, whichever framework, cloud and stack you want to use. A key component is the ability to deploy AI models on a versatile choice of hardware. Through our collaboration with AMD, for about a year now, we are investing into multiple different accelerators such as AMD Instinct™ and Radeon™ GPUs, EPYC™ and Ryzen™ CPUs and Ryzen AI NPUs helping ensure there will always be a device to run the largest AI community on the AMD fleet. Today we are delighted to announce that Hugging Face and AMD have been hard at work together to enable the latest generation of AMD GPU servers, namely AMD Instinct MI300, to have first-class citizen integration in the overall Hugging Face Platform. From prototyping in your local environment, to running models in production on Azure ND Mi300x V5 VMs, you don't need to make any code change using transformers[1], text-generation-inference and other libraries, or when you use Hugging Face products and solutions - we want to make it super easy to use AMD MI300 on Hugging Face and get the best performance. Let’s dive in!

With so many things happening right now in AI it was absolutely necessary to make sure the MI300 line-up is correctly tested and monitored in the long-run. To achieve this, we have been working closely with the infrastructure team here at Hugging Face to make sure we have robust building blocks available for whoever requires to enable continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) and to be able to do so without pain and without impacting the others already in place.

According to recent reports, to enable such things, we worked together with AMD and Microsoft Azure teams to leverage the recently introduced Azure ND MI300x V5 as the building block targeting MI300. In a couple of hours our infrastructure team was able to deploy, setup and get everything up and running for us to get our hands on the MI300!

In a recent development, we also moved away from our old infrastructure to a managed Kubernetes cluster taking care of scheduling all the Github workflows Hugging Face collaborators would like to run on hardware specific pods. This migration now allows us to run the exact same CI/CD pipeline on a variety of hardware platforms abstracted away from the developer. We were able to get the CI/CD up and running within a couple of days without much effort on the Azure MI300X VM.

Industry observers note that as a result, transformers and text-generation-inference are now being tested on a regular basis on both the previous generation of AMD Instinct GPUs, namely MI250 and also on the latest MI300. In practice, there are tens of thousands of unit tests which are regularly validating the state of these repositories ensuring the correctness and robustness of the integration in the long run.

As said in the prelude, we have been working on enabling the new AMD Instinct MI300 GPUs to efficiently run inference workloads through our open source inferencing solution, text-generation-inference (TGI) TGI can be seen as three different components: - A transport layer, mostly HTTP, exposing and receiving API requests from clients - A scheduling layer, making sure these requests are potentially batched together (i.e. continuous batching) to increase the computational density on the hardware without impacting the user experience - A modeling layer, taking care of running the actual computations on the device, leveraging highly optimized routines involved in the model.

Here, with the help of AMD engineers, we focused on this last component, the modeling, to effectively setup, run and optimize the workload for serving models as the Meta Llama family. In particular, we focused on: - Flash Attention v2 - Paged Attention - GPTQ/AWQ compression techniques - PyTorch integration of ROCm TunableOp - Integration of optimized fused kernels.

Most of these have been around for quite some time now, FlashAttention v2, PagedAttention and GPTQ/AWQ compression methods (especially their optimized routines/kernels). We won’t detail the three above and we invite you to navigate to their original implementation page to learn more about it.

Still, with a totally new hardware platform, new SDK releases, it was notable to carefully validate, profile and optimize every bit to make sure the user gets all the power from this new platform.

Industry observers note that last but not least, as part of this TGI release, we are integrating the recently released AMD TunableOp, part of PyTorch 2.3. TunableOp provides a versatile mechanism which will look for the most efficient way, with respect to the shapes and the data type, to execute general matrix-multiplication (i.e. GEMMs). TunableOp is integrated in PyTorch and is still in active development but, as you will see below, makes it possible to improve the performance of GEMMs operations without significantly impacting the user-experience. Specifically, we gain a 8-10% speedup in latency using TunableOp for small input sequences, corresponding to the decoding phase of autoregressive models generation.

In fact, when a new TGI instance is created, we launch an initial warming step which takes some dummy payloads and makes sure the model and its memory are being allocated and are ready to shine.

With TunableOp, we enable the GEMM routine tuner to allocate some time to look for the most optimal setup with respect to the parameters the user provided to TGI such as sequence length, maximum batch size, etc. When the warmup phase is done, we disable the tuner and leverage the optimized routines for the rest of the server’s life.

As stated previously, we ran all our benchmarks using Azure ND MI300x V5, recently introduced at Microsoft BUILD, which integrates eight AMD Instinct GPUs onboard, against the previous generation MI250 on Meta Llama 3 70B, deployment, we observe a 2x-3x speedup in the time to first token latency (also called prefill), and a 2x speedup in latency in the following autoregressive decoding phase.

TGI latency results for Meta Llama 3 70B, comparing AMD Instinct MI300X on an Azure VM against the previous generation AMD Instinct MI250.

According to recent reports, hugging Face libraries can as well be used to fine-tune models. We use Transformers and PEFT libraries to finetune Llama 3 70B using low rank adapters (LoRA. To handle the parallelism over several devices, we leverage DeepSpeed Zero3 through Accelerate library.

On Llama 3 70B, our workload consists of batches of 448 tokens, with a batch size of 2. Using low rank adapters, the model’s original 70,570,090,496 parameters are frozen, and we instead train an additional subset of 16,384,000 parameters thanks to low rank adapters.

From our comparison on Llama 3 70B, we are able to train about 2x times faster on an Azure VM powered by MI300X, compared to an HPC server using the previous generation AMD Instinct MI250.

It has been revealed that moreover, as the MI300X benefits from its 192 GB HBM3 memory (compared to 128 GB for MI250), we manage to fully load and fine-tune Meta Llama 3 70B on a single device, while an MI250 GPU would not be able to fit in full the ~140 GB model on a single device, in float16 nor bfloat16. Because it’s always important to be able to replicate and challenge a benchmark, we are releasing a companion Github repository containing all the artifacts and source code we used to collect performance showcased in this blog.

We have a lot of exciting features in the pipe for these new AMD Instinct MI300 GPUs. One of the major areas we will be investing a lot of efforts in the coming weeks is minifloat (i.e. float8 and lower). These data layouts have the inherent advantages of compressing the information in a non-uniform way alleviating some of the complications faced with integers.

In a recent development, in scenarios like inferencing on LLMs this would divide by two the size of the key-value cache usually used in LLM. Later on, combining float8 stored key-value cache with float8/float8 matrix-multiplications, it would bring additional performance benefits along with reduced memory footprints.

As you can see, AMD MI300 brings a significant boost of performance on AI use-cases covering end-to-end use cases from training to inference. We, at Hugging Face, are very excited to see what the community and enterprises will be able to achieve with these latest hardware and integrations. We are eager to hear from you and help in your use-cases.

Make sure to stop by optimum-AMD and text-generation-inference Github repositories to get the latest performance optimization towards AMD GPUs!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When building AI systems, open models is the best solution to meet security, compliance and privacy requirements of enterprises:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we announce the Dell Enterprise Hub, a new experience on Hugging Face to easily train and deploy open models on-premise using Dell platforms.

Try it out at dell.huggingface.co.

When building AI systems, open models is the best solution to meet security, compliance and privacy requirements of enterprises:.

But working with large language models (LLMs) within on-premises infrastructure often requires weeks of trial and error, dealing with containers, parallelism, quantization and out of memory errors.

With the Dell Enterprise Hub, we make it easy to train and deploy LLMs on premise using Dell platforms, reducing weeks of engineering work into minutes.

The Dell Enterprise Hub offers a curated list of the most advanced open models available today, including Llama 3 from Meta, Mixtral from Mistral AI, Gemma from Google and more.

To access Dell Enterprise Hub, all you need is a Hugging Face account.

The Dell Enterprise Hub is designed from the ground up for enterprises, and optimized for Dell Platforms.

You can easily filter available models by their license or model size.

Sources indicate that once you’ve selected a model, you can review a comprehensive model card designed for enterprise use. At a glance you see key information about the model, its size, and which Dell platforms support it well.

Many models from Meta, Mistral and Google require authorization to get access to the model weights. Because Dell Enterprise Hub is built upon Hugging Face user accounts, your account entitlements transfer over to Dell Enterprise Hub, and you only need to get permission once.

Once you’ve selected a deployable model, deploying it in your Dell environment is really easy. Just select a supported Dell platform, and the number of GPUs you want to use for your deployment.

When you paste the provided script in your Dell environment terminal or server, everything happens automagically to make your model available as an API endpoint hosted on your Dell platform. Hugging Face optimized deployment configurations for each Dell platform, taking into account the available hardware, memory and connectivity capabilities, and regularly tests them on Dell infrastructure to offer the best results out of the box.

Industry observers note that fine-tuning models improves their performance on specific domains and use cases by updating the model weights based on manufacturer-specific training data. Fine-tuned open models have been shown to outperform the best available closed models like GPT-4, providing more efficient and performant models to power specific AI features. Because the company-specific training data often includes confidential information, intellectual property and customer data, it is vital for enterprise compliance to do the fine-tuning on-premises, so the data never leaves the company secure IT environment.

Sources indicate that fine-tuning open models on premises with Dell Enterprise Hub is just as easy as deploying a model. The main additional parameters are to provide the optimized training container with the Dell environment local path where the training dataset is hosted, and where to upload the fine-tuned model when done. Training datasets can be provided as CSV or JSONL formatted files, following this specification.

What if you want to deploy on-premises your own model without it ever leaving your secure environment?

With the Dell Enterprise Hub, once you’ve trained a model it will be hosted in your local secure environment at the path you selected. Deploying it is just another simple step by selecting the tab “Deploy Fine-Tuned”.

And if you trained your model on your own using one of the model architectures supported by Dell Enterprise Hub, you can deploy it the exact same way.

Just set the local path to where you stored the model weights in the environment you will run the provided code snippet.

Recent findings suggest that once deployed, the model is available as an API endpoint that is easy to call by sending requests following the OpenAI-compatible Messages API. This makes it super easy to transition a prototype built with OpenAI to a secure on-premises deployment set up with Dell Enterprise Hub.

Today we are very excited to release the Dell Enterprise Hub, with many models available as ready-to-use containers optimized for many platforms, 6 months after announcing our collaboration with Dell Technologies.

Dell offers many platforms built upon AI hardware accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel Gaudi. Hugging Face engineering collaborations with NVIDIA (optimum-nvidia), AMD (optimum-amd) and Intel (optimum-intel and optimum-habana) will allow us to offer ever more optimized containers for deployment and training of open models on all Dell platform configurations. We are excited to bring support to more state-of-the-art open models, and enable them on more Dell platforms - we’re just getting started!

Industry observers note that spaces Dev Mode lets you connect with VS Code or SSH directly to your Space. It has been revealed that for example, let’s change the color theme of this Gradio Space. After editing the code, no need to push your changes and rebuild the Space container to test it. Go directly in your Space and click “Refresh”.

That’s it! Once you’re satisfied with your changes, you can commit and merge to persist them.

Tech Report: Deploy models on AWS Inferentia2 from Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AWS Inferentia2 is the latest AWS machine learning chip available through the Amazon EC2 Inf2 instances on Amazon Web Services.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have been working for over a year with the product and engineering teams at AWS to make the performance and cost-efficiency of AWS Trainium and Inferentia chips available to Hugging Face users.
  • Today, we are making the power of Inferentia2 directly and widely available to Hugging Face Hub consumers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AWS Inferentia2 is the latest AWS machine learning chip available through the Amazon EC2 Inf2 instances on Amazon Web Services. Designed from the ground up for AI workloads, Inf2 instances offer great performance and cost/performance for production workloads.

Recent findings suggest that we have been working for over a year with the product and engineering teams at AWS to make the performance and cost-efficiency of AWS Trainium and Inferentia chips available to Hugging Face users. Our open-source library optimum-neuron makes it easy to train and deploy Hugging Face models on these accelerators. You can read more about our work accelerating transformers, large language models and text-generation-inference (TGI).

Today, we are making the power of Inferentia2 directly and widely available to Hugging Face Hub consumers.

A few months ago, we introduced a new way to deploy Large Language Models (LLMs) on SageMaker, with a new Inferentia/Trainium option for supported models, like Meta Llama 3. You can deploy a Llama3 model on Inferentia2 instances on SageMaker to serve inference at scale and benefit from SageMaker’s complete set of fully managed features for building and fine-tuning models, MLOps, and governance.

Today, we are expanding support for this deployment experience to over 100,000 public models available on Hugging Face, including 14 newly introduced model architectures (albert,bert,camembert,convbert,deberta,deberta-v2,distilbert,electra,roberta,mobilebert,mpnet,vit,xlm,xlm-roberta), and 6 new machine learning tasks (text-classification,text-generation,token-classification,fill-mask,question-answering,feature-extraction).

Following these simple code snippets, AWS customers will be able to easily deploy the models on Inferentia2 instances in Amazon SageMaker.

According to recent reports, the easiest option to deploy models from the Hub is Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Today, we are happy to introduce newly introduced Inferentia 2 instances for Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. So now, when you find a model in Hugging Face you are interested in, you can deploy it in just a few clicks on Inferentia2. All you need to do is select the model you want to deploy, select the new Inf2 instance option under the Amazon Web Services instance configuration, and you’re off to the races.

For supported models like Llama 3, you can select 2 flavors:.

Hugging Face Inference Endpoints are billed by the second of capacity used, with cost scaling up with replica autoscaling, and down to zero with scale to zero - both automated and enabled with easy to use settings.

Inference Endpoints uses Text Generation Inference for Neuron (TGI) to run Llama 3 on AWS Inferentia. TGI is a purpose-built solution for deploying and serving Large Language Models (LLMs) for production workloads at scale, supporting continuous batching, streaming and much more. In addition, LLMs deployed with Text Generation Inference are compatible with the OpenAI SDK Messages API, so if you already have Gen AI applications integrated with LLMs, you don’t need to change the code of your application, and just have to point to your upcoming endpoint deployed with Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

After you deploy your endpoint on Inferentia2, you can send requests using the Widget provided in the UI or the OpenAI SDK.

We are working hard to expand the scope of models enabled for deployment on AWS Inferentia2 with Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Next, we want to add support for Diffusion and Embedding models, so you can generate images and build semantic search and recommendation systems leveraging the acceleration of AWS Inferentia2 and the ease of use of Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

In a recent development, in addition, we continue our work to improve performance for Text Generation Inference (TGI) on Neuronx, ensuring faster and more efficient LLM deployments on AWS Inferentia 2 in our open source libraries. Stay tuned for these updates as we continue to enhance our capabilities and optimize your deployment experience!

CyberSecEval 2 - A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Cybersecurity Risks and Capabilities of Large Language Models

📅 24 May 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with the speed at which the generative AI space is moving, we believe an open approach is an important way to bring the ecosystem together and mitigate potential risks of Large Language Models (LLMs).
  • CyberSecEval 2 benchmarks help evaluate LLMs’ propensity to generate insecure code and comply with requests to aid cyber attackers:.
  • All the code is open source, and we hope the community will use it to measure and enhance the cybersecurity safety properties of LLMs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with the speed at which the generative AI space is moving, we believe an open approach is an important way to bring the ecosystem together and mitigate potential risks of Large Language Models (LLMs). Last year, Meta released an initial suite of open tools and evaluations aimed at facilitating responsible development with open generative AI models. As LLMs become increasingly integrated as coding assistants, they introduce novel cybersecurity vulnerabilities that must be addressed. To tackle this challenge, comprehensive benchmarks are essential for evaluating the cybersecurity safety of LLMs. This is where CyberSecEval 2, which assesses an LLM's susceptibility to code interpreter abuse, offensive cybersecurity capabilities, and prompt injection attacks, comes into play to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of LLM cybersecurity risks. You can view the CyberSecEval 2 leaderboard here.

CyberSecEval 2 benchmarks help evaluate LLMs’ propensity to generate insecure code and comply with requests to aid cyber attackers:.

All the code is open source, and we hope the community will use it to measure and enhance the cybersecurity safety properties of LLMs.

You can read more about all the benchmarks here.

Our latest evaluation of state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) using CyberSecEval 2 reveals both progress and ongoing challenges in addressing cybersecurity risks.

Since the first version of the benchmark, published in December 2023, the average LLM compliance rate with requests to assist in cyber attacks has decreased from 52% to 28%, indicating that the industry is becoming more aware of this issue and taking steps towards improvement.

It has been revealed that we found models without code specialization tend to have lower non-compliance rates compared to those that are code-specialized. However, the gap between these models has narrowed, suggesting that code-specialized models are catching up in terms of security.

Recent findings suggest that our prompt injection tests reveal that conditioning LLMs against such attacks remains an unsolved problem, posing a significant security risk for applications built using these models. Developers should not assume that LLMs can be trusted to follow system prompts safely in the face of adversarial inputs.

Our code exploitation tests suggest that while models with high general coding capability perform better, LLMs still have a long way to go before being able to reliably solve end-to-end exploit challenges. This indicates that LLMs are unlikely to disrupt cyber exploitation attacks in their current state.

It has been revealed that our interpreter abuse tests highlight the vulnerability of LLMs to manipulation, allowing them to perform abusive actions inside a code interpreter. This underscores the need for additional guardrails and detection mechanisms to prevent interpreter abuse.

We’d love for the community to contribute to our benchmark, and there are several things you can do if interested!

It has been revealed that to run the CyberSecEval 2 benchmarks on your model, you can follow the instructions here. Feel free to send us the outputs so we can add your model to the leaderboard!

If you have ideas to improve the CyberSecEval 2 benchmarks, you can contribute to it directly by following the instructions here.

Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE). Falcon 2: An 11B parameter pretrained language model and VLM, trained on over 5000B tokens and 11 languages

📅 24 May 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TII is launching a newly introduced generation of models, Falcon 2, focused on providing the open-source community with a series of smaller models with enhanced performance and multi-modal support.
  • The first generation of Falcon models, featuring Falcon-40B and Falcon-180B, made a significant contribution to the open-source community, promoting the release of advanced LLMs with permissive licenses.
  • Recent findings suggest that the second generation of models is focused on increased usability and integrability, building a multi-modal ecosystem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TII is launching a newly introduced generation of models, Falcon 2, focused on providing the open-source community with a series of smaller models with enhanced performance and multi-modal support. Our goal is to enable cheaper inference and encourage the development of more downstream applications with improved usability.

The first generation of Falcon models, featuring Falcon-40B and Falcon-180B, made a significant contribution to the open-source community, promoting the release of advanced LLMs with permissive licenses. More detailed information on the previous generation of Falcon models can be found in the RefinedWeb, Penedo et al., 2023 and The Falcon Series of Open Language Models, Almazrouei et al., 2023 papers, and the Falcon and Falcon-180B blog posts.

Recent findings suggest that the second generation of models is focused on increased usability and integrability, building a multi-modal ecosystem. We start this journey by releasing not only the base 11B LLM, but also the 11B VLM model that incorporates image understanding capabilities. The vision-language model, or VLM, will allow owners to engage in chats about visual content using text.

As with our previous work, the models offer support mainly in English but have good capabilities in ten other languages, including Spanish, French, and German.

Industry observers note that falcon2-11B was trained on over 5,000 GT (billion tokens) of RefinedWeb, a high-quality filtered and deduplicated web dataset, enhanced with curated corpora. It followed a four-stage training strategy. The first three stages were focused on increasing the context length, from 2048 to 4096 and finally to 8192 tokens. The last stage aimed to further enhance performance using only high-quality data.

Overall, the data sources included RefinedWeb-English, RefinedWeb-Europe (cs, de, es, fr, it, nl, pl, pt, ro, sv), high-quality technical data, code data, and conversational data extracted from public sources.

The training stages were as follows:.

The data was tokenized with Falcon2-11B tokenizer, the same tokenizer as for the previous Falcon models.

The following table summarizes some of the crucial details about the model architecture:.

Falcon2-11B was trained on 1024 A100 40GB GPUs for the majority of the training, using a 3D parallelism strategy (TP=8, PP=1, DP=128) combined with ZeRO and Flash-Attention 2.

Performance on Open LLM Leaderboard tasks:.

The Hugging Face Leaderboard team provided an official evaluation of our model on the Open LLM Leaderboard tasks. The model performs better than models such as Llama3-8B (trained on three times more data) and Mistral-7B, and on par with Gemma-7b.

The evaluation results show that the Falcon2-11B demonstrates similar performance to Falcon-40B, at a four times smaller model size!

Sources indicate that using the Multilingual LLM leaderboard, we compare the Falcon2-11B model to the Llama-7B and Bloom-7B. For reference, we also include Falcon-40B (that supports the same languages), Falcon-7B (that supports French) and Mistral-7B.

Sources indicate that in the spirit of the original Falcon models, the Falcon2-11B was trained not only on English data but also on ten other languages. Our multilingual evaluation results show that the model presents good capabilities in the six languages (de, es, fr, it, nl, ro) featured on the Multilingual LLM Leaderboard and actually shows higher performance than the Falcon-40B and several other multilingual models on all the cited languages.

We will soon release more extensive evaluation results for multilingual capabilities in the Falcon2-11B model card!

We check the model's performance on code generation against the BigCode Leaderboard on the HumanEval benchmark for the Python language, obtaining pass@1 of 29.59%.

And then, you'd run text generation using code like the following:.

Falcon2-11B VLM is a vision-language model (VLM) built on top of the LLM, that additionally handles image inputs and is capable of answering queries about the images. To achieve this, we integrate the pretrained CLIP ViT-L/14 vision encoder with our Falcon2-11B chat-finetuned model, and train with image-text data.

To enhance the VLM's perception of fine-grained details w.r.t small objects in images, we employ a dynamic encoding mechanism at high-resolution for image inputs, similar to LLaVA-Next.

The training is done in two stages: pretraining and finetuning. In both stages, the visual encoder weights are kept frozen. In the pretraining stage, the LLM is kept frozen, and only the multimodal projector is trained on 558K image-caption pairs. This enables the multimodal projector to learn a mapping from visual to text embedding space. During finetuning, both the projector and LLM weights are trained on a corpus of 1.2M image-text instruction data from public datasets, which also includes multi-round conversations.

According to recent reports, the Falcon 2 models are made available under the TII Falcon 2 License, a permissive Apache 2.0-based software license which includes an acceptable use policy that promotes the responsible use of AI. This license was crafted within the spirit of TII's commitment to the open source community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CISA has added two newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
  • It has been revealed that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

It has been revealed that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

In a recent development, on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

It has been revealed that rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

Sources indicate that we're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#6780. Tech Report: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1862 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • According to recent reports, I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

According to recent reports, I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

Recent findings suggest that my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Sources indicate that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

Sources indicate that llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

Sources indicate that vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's massive batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Sources indicate that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Sources indicate that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

Recent findings suggest that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

According to recent reports, strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the massive model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

Industry observers note that all of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

Sources indicate that first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

It has been revealed that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Recent findings suggest that experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

Recent findings suggest that the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

In a recent development, the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

Sources indicate that the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Industry observers note that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

According to recent reports, most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Industry observers note that most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

According to recent reports, it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Sources indicate that beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Industry observers note that finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

View CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released latest versions for several affected products and recommends to patch to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. Industry observers note that on October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to patch to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Automation Software Products are affected:.

Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC are affected: SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC PCS 7 V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V17 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V18 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V19 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V20 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V21 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V7.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.0 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 1 Vulnerability Weak Authentication Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Firm Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-58114 Affected systems do not properly secure their remote user authentication with the deprecated NTLM protocol. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers, who have achieved a machine in the middle position, to relay NTLM authentication and impersonate a legitimate user. The potential impact depends on the services that are accessible, e.g. a SQL server used by WinCC. #6771. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Fresh Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2106 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Fresh Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Sources indicate that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Sources indicate that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

According to recent reports, foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Sources indicate that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

Sources indicate that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

In a recent development, businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that revision at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

In a recent development, figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

According to recent reports, figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

Sources indicate that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

Sources indicate that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

In a recent development, figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

Industry observers note that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a latest cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

Industry observers note that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

In a recent development, figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

In a recent development, A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each latest reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

It has been revealed that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

Sources indicate that A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

According to recent reports, with AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as newly introduced sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

Sources indicate that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

According to recent reports, figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

It has been revealed that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

In a recent development, an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

In a recent development, if a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

Recent findings suggest that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

According to recent reports, figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Industry observers note that figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

According to recent reports, figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

According to recent reports, banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

In a recent development, airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models.
  • Sources indicate that with v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI.
  • According to recent reports, in this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect.

Sources indicate that with v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key.

According to recent reports, in this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling.

Industry observers note that amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs. Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model.

Industry observers note that in older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with type = "openai" or type = "openai_responses". These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional base_url and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key. The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage.

The native provider changes that setup:.

Sources indicate that AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This upcoming path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately.

The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps:.

Industry observers note that the CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. The ephemeral API keys generated by the provider are valid for up to 12 hours or your AWS session length, whichever is shorter.

For this walkthrough, we use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example model, accessed through global cross-Region inference for broadest availability and lowest cost. Review the Amazon Bedrock pricing to understand expected costs before using the model.

It has been revealed that the following example IAM policy grants the permissions used by this walkthrough, for the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model and global inference profile only. Replace ${AWS_REGION} with your source Region (for example, us-west-2 for US West Oregon) and ${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID} with your 12-digit AWS account ID:.

The foundation-model ARN without a Region or account ID is intentional and required for global cross-Region routing. The BedrockInvokeKimiK31DefaultProject statement is only required if using the openai_responses protocol, not with the default openai (Chat Completions).

It has been revealed that security of your AWS environment is a shared responsibility. Review and grant IAM permissions according to the principle of least privilege, particularly for production environments. Consider using a dedicated IAM role for Kimi Code CLI, separate from your regular AWS activities.

After your prerequisites are ready, follow these steps to configure AWS authentication, add the provider and model, and send a test request.

There are different ways to authenticate with the AWS CLI, depending on your organization’s setup. With Named profiles, you can configure multiple AWS contexts and switch between them.

Sources indicate that whichever approach you choose, your session resolves to an IAM identity (user or role) that needs the Amazon Bedrock permissions from the prerequisites. A Region configured in an AWS CLI profile applies to AWS CLI commands, but you must still set the Region explicitly for Kimi Code in Step 2.

According to recent reports, verify that the AWS CLI resolves your intended identity. Omit --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME if you use the default profile:.

Sources indicate that the model alias bedrock-kimi-k3-1 is a local name used by Kimi Code CLI. The model value is the Amazon Bedrock global inference-profile ID. The example declares a 1-million-token context window and explicit reasoning, image-input, and tool-use capabilities. It omits api_key, api_key_env, and AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK, so the provider uses ambient AWS credentials. A configured Amazon Bedrock key would take precedence.

Because you set default_model, the session selects bedrock-kimi-k3-1 automatically. Ask the agent to explain the repository or propose a small change. Review its proposed file modifications and shell commands before approving them.

At the time of writing, the native bedrock provider has several configuration considerations. These practices help you avoid ambiguous status information and mismatched settings.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, Kimi Code’s desktop and web provider-creation interfaces don’t expose all the provider environment fields used by this credential-chain setup. Edit config.toml directly to set up the Amazon Bedrock provider. For further details, refer to Model providers in the Kimi Code documentation.

Sources indicate that kimi Code doesn’t auto-detect the capabilities of most models on Amazon Bedrock, including Kimi models. Check the Amazon Bedrock model card for each target model and explicitly declare its capabilities to let Kimi Code make use of them.

For example, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports always_thinking, thinking, image_in, and tool_use, but not audio_in or video_in, as reflected in the config.toml example shown earlier.

These declarations describe client behavior. You should only include capabilities that are supported for each target model and Amazon Bedrock API endpoint. Validate tool and image workflows for your application rather than relying on the capability labels alone.

Industry observers note that the bedrock provider requires an explicit AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION in Kimi Code’s config.toml or the shell environment. It can’t infer a Region configured only in ~/.aws/config or through aws configure.

When you use cross-Region inference profiles (with prefixes such as global., us., or in.), the configured Kimi Code Region controls the source Region that receives your requests. For more information, refer to cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

It has been revealed that for workloads without data-residency requirements, start with the global inference profile. This model, like many others, is priced 10% lower for global inference than through geographic profiles. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing for current rates and geographic alternatives.

Industry observers note that in some cases, the provider’s auto-detection might mistake the API protocol or target URL you want to use for a particular model. For example, you will need to set a different URL to use Amazon Bedrock through a VPC endpoint or the Mantle endpoints.

In the Kimi Code config.toml, you can:.

In the following example, we show a configuration to connect to the same model but using the OpenAI Responses API through an Amazon Bedrock VPC endpoint you’ve set up:.

In the Kimi Code desktop and web apps, the provider list can show connected for a bedrock provider. That status doesn’t validate the configured AWS credentials, IAM permissions, Region, model access, or network path. Don’t treat it as proof of a successful model request. Use the non-interactive prompt to test the complete path, and diagnose the actual response if it fails.

If you created a new AWS IAM identity or assigned new permissions to experiment with Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, remember to delete them when you’re finished testing.

In a recent development, you might also want to revert any local Kimi Code CLI provider configurations or AWS CLI profiles you set up. You can even uninstall the CLIs altogether if they’re no longer required. See the uninstall guides for Kimi Code and AWS CLI for details. Remember that deleting the local AWS configuration or CLI doesn’t by itself revoke IAM permissions or an active AWS session.

Amazon Bedrock inference for the models we highlighted is charged on a per-token basis, so there’s no persistent cloud infrastructure deployment to clean up.

According to recent reports, we indicated how Moonshot AI’s native bedrock provider in Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 connects to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock through the standard AWS credential chain. You no longer need a separately managed Amazon Bedrock API key.

In a recent development, amazon Bedrock gives you access to open and proprietary AI models from leading providers, through standard APIs. Its governance controls and compliance validation programs can support even strictly regulated workloads.

If you’re already using Kimi Code CLI and want to run inference on AWS, upgrade today and give the newly introduced streamlined authentication a try.

Industry observers note that for more information about Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, see our launch blog post and the Moonshot AI on AWS samples repository. To explore supported APIs and features by model, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

View CSAF Summary ROS# before version 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that could allow an attacker that is able to pass a crafted message definition file to the user to inject arbitrary code into the generated program. Siemens has released a new version for ROS# and recommends to upgrade to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens ROS# are affected: ROS# vers:intdot/<2.3.1 (CVE-2026-109097) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.2 Siemens ROS# 1 Vulnerability Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109097 Affected systems do not properly escape text of message definition files. This could allow an attacker that is able to pass a crafted message definition file to the user to inject arbitrary code into the generated program. Read More 1 Affected Product ROS# < V2.3.1 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V2.3.1 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-94 Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 8.2 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.
